t: to bless after eating food. The Grace after Meals, said after eating bread. It is possible that this commandment also includes the blessing 'me'ein shalosh' said after food made of the five species of grain (see below 3:11).
and by rabbinic enactment. An enactment of the Sages.
an olive-bulk. Which is the eating measure for many laws.
to bless over every food first. Before eating.
and likewise if he smelled a good fragrance. For the blessings on fragrances see below chapter 9.
any amount. A minimal measure.

and anyone who benefits without a blessing has committed me'ilah. As though he derived forbidden benefit from an object belonging to God (consecrated property), since the earth and its fullness belong to God.
it is rabbinic to bless after anything he eats. Even if it is not 'food'.
a revi'it. Which is the drinking measure everywhere.
and tasting. Eating meant only to test the flavor (and see Hilchot Ta'aniyot 1:14).
up to a revi'it. And beyond this amount it is not tasting but eating.
over every commandment. This too is an enactment of the Sages, so that he direct his heart to the Creator when performing the commandment (and many of these are detailed below in chapter 11).
and the Sages enacted many blessings. To be said on various occasions worthy of note (see below chapter 10).
to always remember the Creator and fear Him. As we repeatedly mention that everything comes from His power and His constant providence over us.
Ezra and his court enacted them. At the beginning of the Second Temple period.
and it is not fitting to change them etc.. In the wording of the blessing and its form.
and anyone who changes the coin that the Sages minted. One who blesses not according to the form the Sages fixed for that blessing (see also Hilchot Keriat Shema 1:7).
mention of the Name and kingship. The name of God and His being King of the world. On this basis the wording for opening the blessing was fixed: 'Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe.'
juxtaposed to its fellow. Attached to another blessing in which the Name and kingship were mentioned.
in any language. In any tongue.
and if he changed the coin etc.. That he did not say it in the form the Sages enacted, but kept the subject of the blessing and the mention of the Name and kingship.
even in a secular language. In a foreign tongue, which is not the holy tongue.
must make his own ear hear. That he read aloud until he hears his words (see also Hilchot Keriat Shema 2:8).
whether he uttered with his lips. In a whisper.
or blessed in his heart. In his thought.
and whether over a thing over which one blesses. The thing of enjoyment or the commandment.
a second time. Again.
bring salt etc.. For all these are for the needs of the meal and are connected to the item over which one blesses (see below 7:3).
give food to the animal. For it is proper to feed the animals before the meal (Hilchot Avadim 9:8), and therefore it is considered a need of the meal.

it is permitted for the unclean to bless them etc.. For impurity does not impair the ability to bless at all, even if it is possible to purify from it and bless in a state of purity (see also Hilchot Tefillah 4:4-5).

and the one who blesses is forbidden to bless while naked. They learned this from the verse 'and He shall not see in you anything unseemly' (Deuteronomy 23:15), not to mention the Name in front of nakedness (see Hilchot Keriat Shema 3:16-17).
sitting with her face to the ground. In a way that her nakedness is fully covered (see also Hilchot Bikkurim 5:11).
he is permitted to bless for others etc.. For the blessing relates to the commandment itself.
except for the blessing of enjoyment, which contains no commandment. For the blessing relates to bodily enjoyment, and therefore a person who did not enjoy does not fulfill the obligation of others.

a blessing of enjoyment that contains a commandment. A blessing over eating that involves a commandment; although it is a blessing over enjoyment, its law is that of a blessing over a commandment (see Responsa of Rambam, no. 253).
and intended to fulfill his obligation with it. That he is obligated in that blessing and wishes to be exempted by his fellow's blessing.
and anyone who answers amen... is like the one who blesses. As if he himself had blessed (see Hilchot Shevuot 2:1).

provided that the one who blesses is obligated in that blessing. For if he is not obligated, the blessing is in vain and one does not fulfill an obligation with it even if they answer amen (below, halakhah 15).

the one who blesses is obligated rabbinically and the one who answers is obligated by Torah law. For example the one who blesses ate bread and was not satisfied, and the listener ate and was satisfied (above 1:1; and see below 5:16).
who gathered. Set themselves to sit together.
they are permitted to eat and drink. For they fulfilled their obligation with his blessing.
in what case does this apply, with bread and wine only. Because of their importance, one blesses for all only if they reclined together.
they do not need reclining. And one exempts the others with his blessing (and see above, halakhah 10).
even though he did not hear the whole blessing. And he is not concerned that perhaps he changed the blessing.
is obligated to answer amen. Because this is an expression of agreement to the praise given to God in the blessing.
a gentile, a heretic or a Samaritan. For it is not known whether they intend to bless God or something else.
a child who is learning. A child learning to bless (below, halakhah 15).
and changed the form of the blessing. That he deviated from the wording and form the Sages enacted (see above, halakhah 6).
a snatched amen. Said before the one blessing finished the blessing.
a cut amen. Truncated, omitting one of its letters.
a short amen. Said very quickly.
medium. Of average length.
among those who answer. Together with others who heard the blessing and answer properly, for he does not fulfill his obligation with it since he did not hear.
an unnecessary blessing. One he is not obligated to say.
takes the Name in vain. For a blessing includes mention of God's Name, and he mentioned it without need.
and he is like one who swears in vain. He is similar to one who swears falsely, who also mentions God's Name in vain, and one who transgresses this should be excommunicated (Hilchot Shevuot 12:9).
and it is forbidden to answer amen after him. For answering amen is as agreement (above, halakhah 11).
the children. Young children.
they teach them the blessings as enacted. As they are said, with the mention of God's Name, which is for the purpose of teaching.
and they do not answer after them etc.. While they are learning, for this is not a blessing (above, halakhah 13).
after his blessings. The blessings he himself blessed.
this is disgraceful. For he appears to be one who did not mean what he said at the start.
the end of the final blessings. The conclusion of a series of blessings that come at the end of a matter (see below, halakhah 17).
this is praiseworthy. For there it is proper to answer amen 'to make known that he has completed all his blessings' (below, halakhah 18).
after 'who builds Jerusalem' in Grace after Meals. The end of the third blessing (see the next halakhah).
and after the last blessing of the evening Shema. But not of the morning one, since it is only one blessing (see below, halakhah 18).
and after it comes the blessing 'who is good and does good'. Which is the fourth blessing of Grace after Meals, and 'who builds Jerusalem' is not 'the end of the final blessings'.
in the days of the Sages of the Mishnah they enacted it. In the generation of Yavneh, whereas the first three blessings were enacted at an earlier time (see below 2:1).
after 'Ahavat Olam'. The second of the blessings of the Shema, before it (Hilchot Keriat Shema 1:6).
the end of the first blessings. Those before the Shema, and one may not interrupt between them and the Shema.
the blessings said before reading the Megillah and lighting the Chanukah lamp. Which are two or three blessings (see Hilchot Megillah ve-Chanukah 1:3; 3:4).
after the blessing over fruits. In the blessing after eating them.

the blessings of a king and the blessings of a high priest. The king at the Hakhel assembly and the high priest on Yom Kippur read from the Torah publicly in the Temple and afterward recite a series of blessings (see Hilchot Chagigah 3:4, Hilchot Avodat Yom ha-Kippurim 3:11).
he does not bless over it, neither at the beginning nor at the end. For a blessing over eating a forbidden thing is blasphemy toward Heaven, not a blessing.
tevel. Produce from which terumot and tithes were not separated (see Hilchot Ma'akhalot Asurot 10:19).
rabbinic tevel. Produce from which the obligation to separate terumot and tithes is rabbinic.
first tithe whose terumah was not all taken. The terumah of the tithe, and sometimes also the great terumah (see Hilchot Terumot 3:13).
second tithe and consecrated items that were not redeemed properly. For the proper manner of redemption see Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni chapter 4, Hilchot Arakhin ve-Charamin chapter 7.
carcasses and torn animals etc.. For in these there is no way to rectify the prohibition.

first tithe whose terumah was taken... provided that he preceded it in the ears. That he separated first tithe in advance while the grain was still in ears, in which case the Levite is exempt from separating great terumah from it and is obligated only in the terumah of the tithe (Hilchot Terumot 3:13), and the tithe is permitted to eat.

even though he did not give the fifth. By law, one who redeems second tithe and consecrated items that are his adds a fifth to the redemption price. But the sanctity was desecrated even if he did not add it, and although ideally he should not eat or benefit until he gives the fifth, he is considered to be eating something that has no prohibition (Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 5:12, Hilchot Arakhin ve-Charamin 7:3).
demai. Produce of the am ha-aretz about which it is not known whether it was tithed, and the Sages enacted to separate from it out of doubt (Hilchot Ma'aser 9:1).

even though it is fit only for the poor. Although the Sages permitted eating demai only to the poor (or to guests - see Hilchot Ma'aser 10:11), nevertheless it is not considered eating something that has a prohibition.
Grace after Meals. Which is recited after eating bread of the five species of grain. For its text see the Order of Prayers, text of Grace after Meals.
the first is the blessing 'who feeds'. A blessing of thanks for God's goodness in sustaining the world.
the second is the blessing of the Land. Thanks for the bestowal of the Land of Israel as an inheritance, and for the food that comes from it.
the third is 'who builds Jerusalem'. A request for mercy for the rebuilding of Jerusalem and the restoration of the kingdom of the House of David.
the fourth is 'who is good and does good'. Thanks for all the good that God bestows on us.
the workers who were doing work etc.. Who were hired, and the Sages were concerned about interrupting the employer's work, and so reduced their obligation in blessings.
they do not bless before it. For this blessing is rabbinic (above 1:2).
only two blessings. Instead of the four mentioned above, halakhah 1.
as enacted. In its entirety.
the second begins with the blessing of the Land etc.. He combines the second and third blessings together, for thanksgiving for Jerusalem is also part of thanksgiving for the Land.

and if they were working during their meal etc.. They receive as their wages only that day's meals. And because their wages are small and there is no great loss in their being idle, they did not enact that they shorten their blessings (see also Hilchot Tefillah 5:8).
or the householder was reclining with them. Eating together with them, in which case the workers bless like him.
a desirable, good and spacious land. For the praise of the Land is the essence of this blessing.
and one must mention in it the covenant and the Torah. The covenant of circumcision and the receiving of the Torah, in whose merit Israel inherited the Land.
for thirteen covenants were made over it. For the word 'covenant' is mentioned thirteen times in the passage commanding circumcision (see Hilchot Milah 3:9).
and over the whole Torah three covenants were made. Over the giving of the entire Torah.

these are the words of the covenant etc., besides the covenant. 'These are the words of the covenant that the Lord commanded Moses to make with the children of Israel in the land of Moab, besides the covenant He made with them at Horeb.' From this verse it is understood that two covenants were made over receiving the Torah and its observance: in the land of Moab and at Horeb (Mount Sinai).
you are standing etc.. This is the third covenant.
and therefore this blessing is called 'nechamah' (consolation). For it mentions expressions of mercy and comfort.
the subject of the blessing. The topic of the blessing.
in the restoration of the kingdom of the House of David. With the coming of the Messiah, who is of the seed of David (see Hilchot Melakhim 11:1).
the sanctity of the day. He mentions the theme of the day.

be pleased and give us rest through Your commandments and the commandment of this seventh day. Be pleased with us and grant us rest in the merit of keeping Your commandments and in the merit of observing the Sabbath.
ya'aleh ve-yavo. A prayer for festivals, which is a request to be remembered before God on these days. For its full text see the Order of Prayers, blessings of the Amidah, section 4.
al ha-nisim. An addition containing thanks for the miracle that occurred at that time. For its full text see the Order of Prayers, blessings of the Amidah, section 7.
he mentions 'retzei ve-hachalitzenu' first. For mention of the Sabbath is more frequent, and therefore comes first.
Rosh Chodesh Tevet that falls on Sabbath. For besides mentioning Sabbath and Rosh Chodesh he must also mention Chanukah.
he must mention in it three kingships. To mention God's kingship three times ('King of the universe... our King... the good King').
he says in the fourth blessing. Instead of the usual text: 'the good King who does good... and all good.'
the living King, the good and doing good etc.. A blessing that includes acceptance of the divine judgment.
and he concludes 'ha-Rachaman'. The conclusion of Grace after Meals.
in the house of grooms. A place where the days of rejoicing after the wedding are celebrated (see Hilchot Ishut 10:12).
and for how long. For how much time.
a widower who married a widow. For both of them this is not a first marriage.
on the first day only. That is the wedding day, since there is not so much rejoicing at such a marriage.
it is the last of the seven wedding blessings. 'Who created joy and gladness,' and those seven blessings are recited at the time of the marriage (Hilchot Ishut 10:3).

if the diners were others... they bless for them after Grace after Meals the seven blessings. For these blessings are said in honor of the assembly that participates in the joy of bride and groom, and therefore if additional guests came who were not present at the time of the blessings, they bless in their honor.
provided that there are ten and the grooms are counted in the number. There must be a quorum, and even the groom himself counts toward the ten (see also Hilchot Ishut 10:5). [
Note:. In the printed editions a halakhah 11 was added here containing the text of the seven blessings. This halakhah is missing in most manuscripts, and was copied here from Hilchot Ishut 10:3.]
the sanctity of the day. The additions 'retzei' or 'ya'aleh ve-yavo' (above, halakhot 5-6).
for a sign and for a holy covenant. For the Sabbath is a sign and covenant between Israel and God (see Exodus 31:16-17).

he remembered after he began the fourth blessing. And this blessing is not part of the essence of Grace after Meals (see above, halakhot 1-2), and therefore once he began it he is considered to have finished Grace after Meals.
he stops. He stops reciting the fourth blessing.

and returns to the beginning, which is the blessing 'who feeds'. For there is an obligation to eat a meal on Sabbath and festivals, and therefore the mention is essential to the blessing (and see also Hilchot Tefillah 10:7, 10:10-11).
for remembrance. For at this time we are remembered before God (see above, halakhah 5, regarding ya'aleh ve-yavo).
and he does not conclude with it. He does not end it with 'Blessed are You, Lord, who sanctifies Israel and the new months,' as he concludes on a festival.
he finishes it and does not return. He completes the fourth blessing, because there is no obligation to eat a meal on Rosh Chodesh.
and likewise on Chol ha-Moed. Its law is the same as Rosh Chodesh, and if he remembers before he began the fourth blessing he says 'Blessed is He who gave...'.
and on Chanukah and Purim, if he forgot etc.. For mention on them is not essential (see Hilchot Tefillah 10:14).
he remembered before the food was digested in his intestines. Before the food was digested, while the person is still satiated from his meal.
it escaped him. He forgot.
he returns and blesses. Because Grace after Meals is a Torah commandment (above 1:1), and a doubt about it is resolved stringently (compare below 8:12).
there are five kinds. They are the five species of grain from which bread is baked.
spelt is of the wheat kind etc.. For they belong to the same category (and see Hilchot Bikkurim 8:4).
when they are ears they are called tevu'ah etc.. And these names apply only to these five species (see Hilchot Nedarim 9:9).
is called bread. That is, loaf.
without an adjective. Wherever bread is mentioned without a qualifying name (such as rice bread), it refers to bread of the five species.
who brings forth bread from the earth. A special praise to God for causing bread, which is a person's staple food, to be produced from the earth.

shaluk. Lightly boiled in water without spices (note of Rabbi Yosef Kafih to Commentary on the Mishnah, Berakhot 6:8; see Commentary on the Mishnah, Terumot 10:11, Hilchot Nedarim 9:1). Some explain that shaluk means cooked a great deal (Rashi, Nedarim 49a and others; see Meiri there, that the word is interpreted in both senses, depending on context).
as it is. The grains whole (compare below, halakhah 4).
who creates the fruit of the earth etc.. By the law of produce of the earth that is customarily eaten cooked (below 8:3).
ate flour. As it is, since it is not customary to eat it that way (see there).
roasted it. Roasted it over fire.
and mixed it with water or other liquids. Made a batter of it.
thick. Dense.
and swallowed it. Ate it, gulped it down.
who creates various kinds of food. By the law of food made of grain.
it was thin. Watery.
shehakol. For there is no merit to grain in being a drink, and its law is like all liquids (below 8:2).
whether alone. For example porridge.
fritters. Cooked dough.
that he split or crushed. Broke the grains into pieces.
groats and Carmel grits. Types of ground grains.
whether bread. He mixed pieces of bread into a cooked dish.
that kind is important to him and was not secondary. The flour or bread was put into the dish as the main ingredient and not for a secondary purpose, as will be explained below, halakhot 6-7.
anything that is primary and with it is something secondary. When he eats two foods together, one of which is secondary to the other.
to bind it. To thicken the dish.
he does not bless over it 'who creates various kinds of food'. Rather the blessing over the vegetable exempts the flour.
but if he mixed it to give flavor in the mixture it is primary. Even though it is a minority, because of the importance of the five species of grain.
wheat starch. Starch.
kinds of sweets. Lumps of candy.
so that the salt not harm his throat and tongue. The fish was too salty to be eaten by itself.
he crumbled it into pieces. Broke it into bits.
there is an olive-bulk in the crumbs. They are still fairly large.
and its form was not changed. Its shape did not dissolve from the cooking.
ha-motzi. For these pieces still have the name of bread.
who creates various kinds of food. By the law of a pot-cooked dish of the five species (above, halakhah 4).
dough baked in the ground. In a pit in the earth, and not in an oven or a vessel.
since it has no form of bread. It does not look like a loaf.
who creates various kinds of food. By the law of food made of grain that is not bread.
and if he set his meal on it. He eats this baked item as the main part of the meal, so that in practice it serves as bread.
dough kneaded with honey etc.. Special kinds of cakes and pastries.
bread that comes as a dessert. Bread that comes as a dessert at the end of the meal.
although it is bread etc.. Although it is defined as bread, one blesses over it 'who creates various kinds of food' because it is not customary to set a meal on it, but it is eaten for pleasure.
rice... who creates various kinds of food. Because rice resembles grain to a great degree and so it is treated as a pot-cooked dish, but it has no importance of bread if baked.
millet. A kind of legume used in a way similar to rice.
at first he blesses shehakol. For these kinds have no special importance.
four blessings. The full Grace after Meals (above 2:1).
one blessing, me'ein shalosh. An abbreviated blessing that includes the main points of Grace after Meals. Its text will be given below, halakhah 13.
from an olive-bulk and up. Which is the eating measure everywhere.
less than a revi'it. Which is the measure of drinking everywhere.
ha-michyah. Things that sustain the body.
ha-kalkalah. Food.
a kind of sanctity of the day. A mention of the sanctified day and a request for salvation on it.
in the place where he stopped. The place where he finished eating.
he sits in his place and blesses. For this is the way of a fixed meal.
and remembered before the food was digested. In which case his law is that he blesses (above 2:14).
in the place where he remembered. Even though he did not eat there.
and if he was deliberate. That he left the place of eating knowing he had not blessed.
and if he blessed in the place where he remembered, he fulfilled his obligation. Even if he left deliberately.
he does not return and bless, because it is not from the Torah. Like all blessings before eating, and only Grace after Meals after eating is from the Torah (above 1:1-2; and see below 8:12).
he returns and blesses. Since he benefited from the continuation of eating.
he does not bless. The first blessing, because he has already finished his eating.
and interrupted his meal and went to another house... since he changed his place. And a change of place is interpreted as finishing the eating (below, halakhah 5).
to bless retroactively. Grace after Meals for what he ate earlier.
and returns and blesses ha-motzi as at first. For the eating after his return is considered a different meal.
and went out toward a groom or toward a bride. An example of a reason that causes all the diners to go out.
left an elder or a sick person there. An example of one of the participants in the meal who did not go out with them.
they return to their place and finish etc.. Since the fixity of the meal was preserved by his not leaving, it is as though they had not finished eating.
and if they did not leave anyone there etc.. They are like an individual who changed his place (above, halakhah 3).

and likewise if they were reclining for drinking or for eating fruit. Their law is as above: if they went out and someone remained there they return to their reclining, and if no one remained they must bless retroactively and going forward.
from corner to corner in one house. For the house is considered entirely one place (see also Hilchot Shabbat 29:8), and only if he left it is it considered an interruption (above, halakhah 3).
ate on the eastern side of a fig tree and came to eat on its western side etc.. Since there are no partitions, the area under the fig tree is not considered one place.
exempted all the accompaniments. Foods meant to be eaten with bread. For setting the meal on bread exempts the things that come within the meal and are secondary to it (see below, halakhah 11).

he blessed over a pot-cooked dish, he exempted the cooked dish. A pot-cooked dish is made of the five species (above 3:4), and it too requires a blessing in that place (above, halakhah 1), and it is considered a fixed meal and exempts things that come in it.

he blessed over the cooked dish, he exempted the pot-cooked dish. Some read: he blessed over the cooked dish, he did not exempt the pot-cooked dish, since a cooked dish has no fixed meal. See Kesef Mishneh.
decided in his heart to stop eating. Decided to finish his eating.
changed his mind. Regretted and changed his opinion.
he returns and blesses. The first blessing before he eats or drinks again.
stopped the whole day. Stopped for a long time without eating or drinking.
come, let us bless Grace after Meals. And thereby announced the end of the meal.
come, let us sanctify the sanctity of the day. And let us begin the Sabbath meal (see Hilchot Shabbat 29:11-12).
they are forbidden to drink until they bless. For they obligated themselves in Grace after Meals (and see below 6:20).
or sanctify. Since they interrupted their meal for Kiddush they obligated themselves in it, and it is forbidden to eat or drink before Kiddush (Hilchot Shabbat 29:5).
they need to return and bless 'who creates the fruit of the vine'. By the law of one who decided in his heart to finish eating, as above, halakhah 7.

but if they said, come let us make Havdalah etc.. For a person may continue his meal even if Sabbath has ended and the time of Havdalah has come, and make Havdalah afterward (Hilchot Shabbat 29:12), and for this reason the announcement of Havdalah is not an end of the meal.
they need not bless the blessing over wine a second time. For the blessing over the vine at the beginning exempts the wines that come afterward.
who is good and does good. Thanks for the special good in having a multiplicity of wines (and see below 10:7 for another case in which this blessing is said).
until it comes before him. That the food be placed before the one who blesses.
he must return and bless. For his mind was not on that food from the start.
and it fell from his hand and burned or a river swept it away. Examples of situations in which he cannot eat it.
and he must say 'Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever' etc.. And so it turns out that the mention of God's Name in the blessing is not in vain, but in order to add praise to it.
an aqueduct. A channel of flowing water.
for this was his intention from the start. For from the beginning he knew that he would drink from the water that would reach him after the blessing.
during the meal and because of the meal. Eaten during the meal, and they are among the things eaten to satisfy.

for everything is secondary to the meal. And the blessing over the primary exempts the secondary (above 3:5-7), and in this case, even if they are not eaten literally together with the bread, they are included in the meal itself and are secondary to it.

that are not because of the meal that came during the meal. Things eaten as dessert for the meal, which are not meant to satisfy but for pleasure, but were eaten during the meal and not after its conclusion.
require a blessing before them. Because they are not secondary to the blessing over the bread.
and do not require a blessing after them. For they are exempted by Grace after Meals, since they are included within the meal.
after the meal. After finishing eating, and before Grace after Meals.
require a blessing before and after them. For they are not part of the meal.
on Sabbaths and festivals. On which one must set the meal on wine (Hilchot Shabbat 30:9, Hilchot Yom Tov 6:18).
and when he comes out of the bathhouse. For at that time there is a health benefit in drinking wine (see Hilchot De'ot 4:17).
that a person sets his meal on wine. He opens his meal by drinking wine, and intends to continue drinking wine also after eating.
exempted the wine he drinks after the meal. For this was his intention from the start.
but on other days he must return and bless first over the wine after the meal. For one who drinks wine after eating is like one who changed his mind (above, halakhah 7).
wine came to them during the meal. To a group who ate together.
each one blesses for himself. And one does not bless for all (compare above 1:12).
since the throat is not free. And they might choke if they answer amen while swallowing (see below 7:6).
and it does not exempt the wine after the meal. For it is like one who changed his mind, as above.

and there is a doubt in the matter etc.. Grace after Meals is not a time-bound positive commandment from which women and slaves are exempt (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 12:3, Hilchot Chagigah 2:1), and therefore they may be obligated in it by Torah law. But it is possible that nevertheless they are not obligated.
therefore they do not exempt the adults. The males who are obligated by Torah law, lest women and slaves are not obligated in the blessing (see below, halakhah 16).

rabbinic, in order to train them. An obligation by rabbinic enactment, to accustom minors to commandments (for further examples see Hilchot Keriat Shema 4:1, Hilchot Tefillin 4:13, Hilchot Tzitzit 3:9 and more).
the blessing of zimmun. A blessing of invitation of the group to bless, as follows.
and afterward he begins and says... and they answer amen. The one inviting recites Grace after Meals, and the other diners listen to him and thereby fulfill their obligation.
from ten and up they invite with the Name. They mention God's Name in the blessing of zimmun.
from when they begin to engage in the needs of a wedding feast etc.. From when they began preparing things for the meal, from that time there is already joy because of the wedding.
for the joy is in His dwelling. For at the time of the joy of the wedding, this is joy also for God in His dwelling.
a meal that is made after the wedding because of the wedding. For the invitees it is said that the meal is held because of the joy of the wedding.
even priests who ate most-holy offerings in the Temple court. Although their eating is for the sake of atonement and not for eating as such (see Hilchot Ma'aseh ha-Korbanot 10:3).
and the priests ate terumah and the Israelites ate secular food. Although Israelites are forbidden to eat terumah, they join in zimmun with the priests.
are obligated in zimmun like their obligation in Grace after Meals. See above, halakhah 1.
they do not invite over them. They do not complete a zimmun of adults.
but they invite for themselves. In a group of their own.
and there must not be a group of women, slaves and minors because of licentiousness. For it is not fitting that they recline to eat together (see also Hilchot Korban Pesach 2:4).
provided that they do not invite with the Name. For they are not counted in a quorum for a matter of holiness (see Hilchot Tefillah 8:4-5).
androgynos. One who has both male and female organs, and the Sages did not decide whether he is treated as male or female (Hilchot Ishut 2:24
invites for his kind. For others who are like him.
and a tumtum. One whose sexual organs are covered, and it is not known whether he is male or female (ibid.). [Note: In the Commentary on the Mishnah Rambam vocalizes this word 'tumtum'.]
does not invite at all. Not even for others like him, lest they be of the other sex.
a minor who knows to whom one blesses. Understands that one gives thanks to God, who is Creator of the world.
who ate an olive-bulk of bread or more. And with this amount he became obligated in Grace after Meals (above 1:1).
brine. Sauce.
they join for zimmun with the Name. For they ate, and they can join and say 'that we have eaten of His food'.
a great majority. A large majority, seven out of ten.

in what case does this apply, with ten. That the joining of those who did not eat bread is for completing the mention of the Name as a matter of holiness, and not because they are counted in the zimmun itself.
and a third came and ate. In the same place.
if they are able to eat with him any amount. If they are capable of eating more, even though they did not actually eat, and thereby it is considered that they have not yet finished their meal.
even of other foods. That are not bread.
joins with them. For he ate with them before the end of the meal.
and the greatest sage among those reclining is the one who blesses. Out of honor for the blessing (see below 7:2).
they may not divide. To bless separately from one another and avoid zimmun.
they may divide. They may divide into small groups of three.
that as long as they divide etc.. They may divide on condition that each group can invite in the same manner that it would invite had they not divided.
they may not divide. Because each of them has already obligated himself in zimmun, rather they invite together even though they did not eat together.
for each one eats from his own. From his own food, and does not give to others.
when some of them see others. When nothing completely hides the groups from each other, they are like one group.
attendant. A waiter.
so that he pays attention to hear what they say. The blessing of zimmun.
and fulfills his obligation. The obligation of zimmun.
and when he returns to his place. See above 4:1.
they do not invite over him until he returns etc.. For it is not fitting to mention the Name of Heaven with fewer than ten.
they invite over him. He joins them for zimmun, although he has blessed.
for there is no retroactive zimmun. For it is an invitation to bless, and is done only before the blessing.
each one blesses for himself. For there is zimmun only with three.
and the second answers... and fulfills his obligation. For a person may exempt his fellow with a blessing he is obligated in (above 1:10).
curse. A curse.
for one whose wife and sons bless for him. For a person who needs it and does not know how to bless by himself.
rabbinic. Above 1:1.

and therefore a minor, slave or woman may exempt them from their obligation. For the minor is obligated rabbinically, and for the woman and slave the degree of obligation is in doubt (above, halakhah 1).
for anyone obligated in a matter by Torah law etc.. Above 1:11; and see Hilchot Shofar 2:2.
let us bless. At the beginning of the blessing of zimmun.
blessed and blessing. For he cannot say 'Blessed is He of whose food we ate' (above, halakhah 2), since he did not eat with them.
blessed is He of whose food we ate. At the end of the blessing of zimmun.
he answers after them amen. An expression of agreement, as with every blessing (above 1:13).
the bread over which one blesses ha-motzi. Its definition was explained above, chapter 3.

washing hands first and last. Rinsing the hands before eating and after it. The Sages decreed that hands be impure for purposes of terumah, and enacted hand washing to purify them (see Hilchot She'ar Avot ha-Tumah 8:8). They then added the obligation also for secular food so that those who eat terumah would become accustomed to wash their hands (Babylonian Talmud, Chullin 106a).
even though his hands are not dirty. For as stated, the washing is not for cleanliness.

something dipped in liquids. A food that is dipped in one of the liquids, and could become impure from the hands through the liquids (Hilchot She'ar Avot ha-Tumah 8:10), and therefore they enacted hand washing before eating it.
whether for eating, for reading the Shema, or for prayer. For at these times there is a commandment to wash hands (see Hilchot Keriat Shema 3:1; Hilchot Tefillah 4:1-2).
it is a commandment of the Sages. An enactment of the Sages.
for we were commanded in the Torah to listen to them. And therefore one can bless 'and commanded us concerning washing hands' (see below 11:3).
and final waters. Which are washed after eating.
for they are only because of danger. They are meant to clean the hands of residues of dangerous salt, and not because of a commandment (see also below 11:4).
therefore a person must be extra careful with them. And be extremely careful with this washing (and see more below, halakhah 3).
between one dish and another. In order to clean oneself of that dish.
and secular fruits etc.. That are not terumah or consecrated items, and do not become impure from the hands (compare Hilchot Terumot 11:7, Hilchot She'ar Avot ha-Tumah 8:8).
this is of the arrogant. The proud, in that he is stringent in a matter where it is unnecessary.
whoever measured the salt. Measured out salt.
at the end. After he finished contact with the salt.
and pass his hands over his eyes and go blind. For it contains substances that may cause blindness.
and in the camp. A military camp, when they go out to and return from war (see Hilchot Melakhim 6:13).
up to the joint. Up to the wrist joint.
a revi'it. For its measure see Hilchot Tefillah 15:4.
for both hands. For both hands together (see also Hilchot Mikva'ot 11:8).
and anything that interposes in immersion. Things stuck to the body that do not allow water to pass (see Hilchot Mikva'ot chapter 2).
and anything that counts toward the measure of a mikveh. Water that is fit to complete the measure of a mikveh, that is not fruit juice or dye water and the like (see Hilchot Mikva'ot 7:1-5).
if he immersed his hands in the water of a mikveh etc.. Suitable for immersion (see Hilchot Mikva'ot 11:1).
that do not have the measure of a mikveh. Which is forty se'ah (ibid. 4:1).
in drawn water in the ground. Water that was drawn and gathered in a pit in the ground, which is invalid for immersion (ibid. 4:2).
he did nothing. For immersion in these does not purify.
in the water itself. The ways of invalidity will be explained below, halakhot 7-9.
and in the measure. The quantity. Above, halakhah 4 and below, halakhah 10.
and in the vessel. That they be poured specifically from a vessel, below halakhot 11-12.
and in the one who pours... by the force of the pourer. That the water not pour by itself, below halakhot 13-14.
a change of appearance. The color of the water.
and uncovering. That the water was uncovered such that a venomous creeping creature might have drunk from it (see Hilchot Rotze'ach 11:11).
and use for work. That the water was used for another purpose.
and loss. Impairment of the quality of the water.
whether in the ground. While still in the ground.
because of their location. For example, they were found in a hot place or one with foul air.
they were uncovered with an uncovering that forbids them for drinking. See there 11:6-16.
in which he soaked his bread. He soaked bread in them to soften it.
rinsed in them vessels that are rinsed, or new ones, did not disqualify them. For this is not considered work.
baker. A baker.
dips loaves in them. He dips the dough in water, and so he performs work with all the water in the vessel.
scoops from them at the time of kneading. Draws from them with the palms of his hands.
the water that he scooped from them remains valid. For no work was done with it.
became slops. Because they were used, they are defined as slop water, which is presumed impure (see Hilchot Tumat Okhalin 2:26, Commentary on the Mishnah, Makhshirin 2:3).
rinsed. Washed.
that became invalid for a dog's drinking. That even a dog cannot drink from them.
and in the ground they are valid for immersion. For the foulness of the water does not disqualify it from the status of a mikveh (Hilchot Mikva'ot 7:1).
the hot springs of Tiberias. Hot springs, whose waters contain sulfur that makes them unfit for drinking. [Note: In the Commentary on the Mishnah Rambam vocalizes this word 'Tiberia'.]
in their place. Where they gush forth, in which they purify like a mikveh.
that he separated from them by a cubit. He divided them by a channel from the spring, and they are not connected.
because they are not fit for animals to drink. For the water of the hot springs of Tiberias is bitter and salty.
the one washing may pour on his hands little by little. He may pour the water slowly.
in one rinse. At once over both his hands (see Hilchot Mikva'ot 11:6).
that they loosen their hands. That the hands not be pressed against one another.
and in that rinse there must be a revi'it for each and every one. Which is the quantity of water for washing for each person (above, halakhah 4; and see also Hilchot Mikva'ot 11:8).
one does not pour on the hands. One may not use any of these as a vessel for washing hands.
with the sides of vessels. Sides broken off earthenware vessels, which have a receptacle.
with the bottom of a deep dish. A deep earthenware base in which vessels are placed.
with shards. That were not made into vessels.
with the stopper of a barrel. A cover for a barrel. All these vessels were not originally made to be receptacles.
he fashioned the stopper for washing. He made it into a vessel meant for washing.
the skin bottle. A leather flask made for keeping liquids.
that he fashioned it. That it could serve for washing.
a sack, a basket etc.. Which are not vessels made to hold liquids.
with his palms. With the palms of his hands.

and vessels that were broken with a breaking that purifies them from impurity. Any vessel that broke after becoming impure, and whose form and use were nullified, is pure through its breaking. And likewise pure vessels that broke, their fragments do not receive impurity (Hilchot Kelim 6:1; for the measure of breaking in vessels of various materials see there chapters 6, 11, 19).
dung vessels and earth vessels. Made of materials of poor quality.
a vessel that does not hold a revi'it. Too small to hold a revi'it.
or that does not contain a revi'it. That has too little water in it (see above, halakhah 6).
even a deaf-mute, an imbecile or a minor. Who are not of sound mind, because the washing need not be done with intent; the act of pouring alone suffices.
he places the vessel between his knees. And tilts it until the water pours out.
or he tilts the barrel over his hands. While it is resting on the ground or the table.
or he washes one hand and pours with it on the other. He pours with one hand onto the other by means of a vessel.
and a monkey may pour for hands. For it too pours the water willingly, and is considered 'the force of a giver' (as above, halakhah 6).
the trough. A hollowed stone meant for holding water.
that a person draws by hand. Draws water and pours it into it.
with a wheel. A machine for drawing water that works by turning a wheel.
with a channel. With a conduit.
there is no one giving on his hands here. For the water flows over his hands by force of its flowing in the channel, although originally a person was the one who drew it into the trough.
if work was done with them. And they are disqualified for washing for that reason (above, halakhah 8).
for any doubt in the purity of hands is pure. Since it is a doubt about a rabbinic enactment (above, halakhah 2; and see also Hilchot Mikva'ot 11:11, Hilchot She'ar Avot ha-Tumah 14:11).
he must raise his hands upward. Turn the fingers upward.
so that the water not go out beyond the joint etc.. For if he turns them downward, water that is outside the joint might return to the hands and make them impure (see also Hilchot Mikva'ot 11:4).
he lowers his hands so that all the force of the salt goes out. He must tilt his fingers downward during the rinse, so that the hands are cleaned completely.
with hot water heated by fire. With hot water that was boiled with fire.
that the hand recoils from. That the hand recoils from this water because of its great heat.
that he cannot rub in them. That it is impossible to clean the hands thoroughly because of the heat of the water.
lukewarm. Slightly warm.
a person washes his hands in the morning and stipulates about them for the whole day. He may wash once in the morning, and stipulate that the washing be effective for the whole day.
diverted his attention. Removed his thought from guarding them (see Hilchot Chametz u-Matzah 8:6).
wrapped. Covered.
in a cloth. A sheet of fabric.
even though he did not wash his hands. For the cloth separates his hands from the food, and it is not liable to become impure (see also Hilchot She'ar Avot ha-Tumah 8:9).
one who feeds others need not wash hands etc.. For the enactment of washing applies only to the person eating.
and the one eating needs hand washing. Lest he touch the food.
with a spatula. With a fork or spoon.
it is forbidden to feed one who did not wash his hands. Because it causes him to transgress an enactment of the Sages.
even though he puts it into his mouth. For this does not exempt the eater from washing (above, halakhah 18).
and it is forbidden to treat hand washing lightly. To take it lightly without justification, just because it is not a Torah commandment.
and the Sages gave many instructions about hand washing. They spoke in praise of those who keep it and in condemnation of those who belittle it.
even if he has only enough water to drink etc.. From this it is understood that it is a very important commandment, and certainly it is not to be belittled.
to wipe his hands. So that they not be wet from the washing water.
like one who eats impure bread. For when one is careful about impurity and purity, one must fear that the water became impure from the hands and makes the bread impure (see Hilchot Mikva'ot 11:3).
at the end. The final waters, at the end of the meal.
wipes and afterward blesses. Out of honor for the blessing.
and must not interrupt between them with anything else. He must not eat or drink at all, because he has become obligated in Grace after Meals (see above 4:8).
and all are matters of etiquette. Customs of courtesy.
the greatest of them all. The most honored person at the meal.
reclining. They recline on couches, leaning on the left side (see Hilchot Chametz u-Matzah 7:8).
and the greatest reclines at the head. First (perhaps meaning he sits on the middle couch, when two couches are arranged in an L shape, and when there are three couches arranged in a U shape).
below him. At the side of the first one's feet.
above him. At the side of the first one's head.
and completes the blessing and afterward breaks. He finishes the blessing while the bread is whole (see below, halakhah 4), and afterward cuts it.
and the guest blesses Grace after Meals. He says the blessing of zimmun and recites Grace after Meals after it (above 5:2-3).
so that he will bless the host. He says the special addition in the fourth blessing (above 2:7).
and if they were all householders. And there are no guests there.
the greatest of them breaks etc.. Out of honor for him.
until they bring salt and a relish. Something to eat with the bread, so that they can begin the meal immediately after the blessing (see above 1:8).
dry bread. Without additions.
like a stingy person. A miser.
like a glutton. A gorger.
he may break a large slice. He is permitted to do so, out of honor for the Sabbath meal.
that is baked well. Fully baked.
from a whole loaf. A whole loaf, which is the honor of the blessing.
a whole one of barley and a slice of wheat. For each has an advantage and a disadvantage.
places the slice inside the whole one. He folds the whole one and puts the slice inside it.
he must break over two loaves. To bless over both, as a remembrance of the double portion of manna that fell in honor of Sabbaths and festivals (see also Hilchot Shabbat 30:9).
the one who breaks gives a slice before each and every one etc.. He places the slice in front of the diner and does not give it to him by hand.
unless he was a mourner. For the custom is that a mourner receives food from others (see Hilchot Avel 4:9).
he is the one who first stretches out his hand. He takes first from the bread, out of honor for him.
to give honor to his teacher etc.. For priority in eating is only a matter of honor, and therefore he may pass it on to another.
two wait for each other at the bowl. When eating from one vessel, so that one not eat before the other.
three do not wait. Two do not wait for one, but follow the majority.
the third interrupts with them. To respond to the blessing of zimmun.
they do not converse. It is forbidden to speak.
so as not to come to danger. The danger of choking, if the windpipe precedes the gullet.
each and every one blesses for himself. See above 4:12.
he does not eat with them. So that he not engage in eating instead of serving the diners.
to put into his mouth. To feed him.
in order to settle his mind. So that he not be distressed.
he blesses over each and every cup. And one blessing at the beginning is not enough.
because his drinking does not depend on his own will but on theirs. And he does not intend to drink more, and his law is that of one who changed his mind (see above 4:7).
washes one hand. Because of the dirt on it.
and extended. Continued for a long time.
washes both hands. Because of diversion of attention (see above 6:17).
they recline for drinking. Without eating.
he enters and sits in his place and washes his hands. Out of cleanliness and etiquette.
turns his face away from the guests. He does not wash facing the guests but turns his back to them, out of respect for them, and after washing he turns back.
and why does he wash in his place. In this case he does not wash outside, but after returning to sit in his place.
they do not leave raw meat etc.. The purpose of these practices is to protect the bread or other foods from spoilage and loss.
and they do not throw the bread. For this is a way of disgrace.
in pipes. Channels.
roasted grain. Roasted wheat.
in the summer. When the ground is dry and not muddy.
that become repulsive. That become dirtied and spoiled for eating.
destroy. Waste and ruin.
a contemptuous way and a kick. As a display of contempt and without need.
lest the host be embarrassed. In a case where there is nothing more than what was placed before the guests.

a person should not send his fellow a barrel of wine with oil floating on its mouth. For they used to pour oil on top of wine, so that it would serve as a separating layer between the wine and the air, which would protect it from souring. When sending a barrel to his fellow, it is forbidden to do so.

lest a person send him a barrel that ran out of oil and he think it is wine. If they were accustomed to send barrels that way, it could cause a mistake. And because they forbade sending, the recipient knows that it is oil and will not err.
and he invites guests and is embarrassed. Because he has nothing to give them to drink.
they remove the table. They used to eat on a small portable table, and at the end of the meal they remove it.
and sweep the place. They sweep the place of bread leftovers.
for it is forbidden to walk on them and wash on them. Because of waste and disgrace of foods (above, halakhah 9).
whoever blesses Grace after Meals. The person who will invite, the guest, or the greatest at the meal (above 5:2).
so that the greatest not sit with his hands soiled etc.. For it is not respectful to him to wait for everyone in such a condition.
and one does not honor in this matter. That one give precedence to one more honored than he to wash before him.
for one does not honor with soiled hands. Rather, if it is a person's turn to wash, he washes. For in a matter enacted because of danger, honor does not apply.
nor on roads nor on bridges. For these too are places of danger, and one does not give precedence to the greatest in them.
but at the doorway fit for a mezuzah and at the time of entering. This is a place fit for honoring.
the incense burner. Kinds of spices burned on coals that they used to smell at the end of the meal.
he blesses over the incense burner. The blessing on spices (below 9:2).
if there was wine there. And they want to recite Grace after Meals over a cup of wine (see below, halakhah 15).
a cup that holds a revi'it or more than a revi'it. Which is the measure fit for a cup of blessing (see Hilchot Shabbat 29:7, Hilchot Chametz u-Matzah 7:7).
and they bring a kind of spice. In honor of the blessing (see Hilchot Ishut 10:4; and see also below 9:4).
pleasant oil and the like. Perfumed oil that must be wiped from the hands.
smeared it on the attendant's head. To perfume his hair.
and if the attendant was a Torah scholar. For it is not fitting for him to go out with perfumed hair (Hilchot De'ot 5:9).
smeared it on the wall. He wipes the oil on the wall.
for Grace after Meals does not require wine. It is not obligatory but one of the practices of a distinguished meal (see Hilchot Chametz u-Matzah 7:10, 8:10).
he must rinse it. A thorough washing.
and fill it with undiluted wine. Not mixed with water.

and when he reaches the blessing of the Land he puts a little water into it. To show the praise of the Land, whose wines are strong and need to be diluted with water (Rabbeinu Yonah on the Rif, Berakhot 37a).
and they do not converse. It is forbidden to speak.
who creates many living things. For the full text of the blessing and its explanation see below, halakhah 8.

of the five species written in the Torah. The kinds of fruit with which the Land of Israel was praised (Deuteronomy 8:8, besides wheat and barley mentioned there, whose law was stated above chapter 3; and compare below, halakhah 13).
one blessing, me'ein shalosh. For the full text of the blessing see below, halakhah 14.
whose growth is not from the earth. Which are not from plants.
not to quench his thirst. But to help him swallow something and the like, in which there is no pleasure of drinking.
he first recites over them "by whose word all things came to be". Because it has changed and no longer has the form of the fruit.
"who creates the fruit of the vine" etc.. Wine has its own special blessing because of the importance of the beverage (see also above 4:9).
and over oil... "who creates the fruit of the tree". The olive was intended from the outset for producing oil, so this is not a change.
has a throat ailment. Feels pain in the throat, and drinking oil helps heal it (see Hilchot Shabbat 21:24).
with the water of cooked vegetables. Water in which vegetables were cooked, which dulls the taste of the oil.

for he did not enjoy the taste of the oil. Since it is not pleasant to drink by itself. And if he had no throat ailment, even if he drank it with the water of cooked vegetables, the oil is secondary to that water and one does not recite a blessing over it.
that are normally eaten raw. That are usually eaten without cooking them.
cooked them. Partial cooking.
he first recites over them "by whose word all things came to be". The blessing proper to a fruit or vegetable is recited only if it is eaten in its usual manner.
he recites a blessing over their cooking water. The water in which the vegetables were cooked, if he drinks it.
date honey. Squeezed from dates, and it has the law of a beverage squeezed from fruit (above halakhah 2).
and made them like dough. Pressed the dates together.
he first recites over them "who creates the fruit of the tree" etc.. Because this is not a significant change.
sweet reeds etc.. Sugar cane.
"who creates the fruit of the ground". As is the law for something that comes from a tree but is not a fruit (such as the caper bud, below halakhah 6).
"who creates the fruit of the tree". Because the sugar is considered the fruit of the cane.
for this is not a fruit. The sugar extracted from the cane by cooking is not in the category of fruit.
the honey of these reeds will not be etc.. For this is certainly a significant change, even more than squeezing.
the heart of the palm, which is like a white tree. It is edible when it is soft.
he first recites over it "by whose word all things came to be". Because the palm was not planted for the sake of eating the heart.
the caper bud of the caper plant. The flower buds of the caper plant, which are edible but are not considered fruit (see also Hilchot Terumot 2:4).
he recites over them "who creates the fruit of the tree". Because the caper berries (aviyonot) are considered fruits of the tree in every respect (see Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 10:3).
fresh. Moist, not dried for use as a spice.
he first recites over them "who creates the fruit of the ground". Because they are fit for eating (see Hilchot Shevitat Asor 2:6).
for they are spices and not food. They are meant to give flavor to other things and are not considered food in themselves (see Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 7:9).
foods that are not fit for eating etc.. For example, one who eats them as medicine, so that he derives no pleasure of taste from them (compare above halakhah 2).
that became moldy. Mold grew on it.
that became sour. Began to turn sour (in another version: "and became rancid").
whose form has changed. It stood for a time and began to spoil.
and the unripe fruit, which are early figs. Fruit that fell from the tree before ripening.
and the locust. A locust, which is kosher to eat (Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 1:21).
"who creates many living beings" over everything that He created etc.. Thanks to God for everything He created and for sustaining all the worlds.

lees onto which he poured three and took out four. Wine lees onto which water was poured in order to extract the wine, and the liquid that came out of the lees exceeded the water that was added in a ratio of four to three.
for this is diluted wine. The usual ratio for mixing wine with water is one measure of wine to three measures of water, and the extra measure that came out is wine that drained from the lees.
took out less than four. In this case not enough wine came out for the drink to be defined as diluted wine.
if he said "who creates the fruit of the ground" he has fulfilled his obligation. Because the tree too grows from the ground.
if he said "who creates the fruit of the tree" he has not fulfilled his obligation. Because this is not the fruit of the tree.
if he recited "by whose word all things came to be" he has fulfilled his obligation. Because it is a blessing that covers everything.
and he erred and said "who creates the fruit of the vine". That the blessing does not match what he intended to drink.
we do not make him repeat. Because we consider only the intention he had at the start of the blessing.
since there was no error in the main part of the blessing. In its important part, which is mentioning the Name and God's kingship.
all these blessings. The blessings over fruits and other foods mentioned in this chapter.
which are rabbinic. By enactment of the Sages (see above 1:1).
swallows them. For there is no possibility of reciting a blessing while they are still in his mouth, and he should not spoil them.
and recites the blessing at the end. The after-blessing (and he does not recite the first blessing, see above 4:2).
for if he throws them away they will become repulsive. If he spits them out of his mouth he will not eat them again.
moves them to one side. To one side of his mouth.
spits them out of his mouth until he recites the blessing, and his mouth is free. Out of respect for the blessing, when this is possible.
many kinds. Many types of food.
equal. The same.

and whichever kind he wishes to put first, he puts first. He should prefer the one he likes best and recite the blessing over it first (this applies both where their blessings are the same and where their blessings are not the same - Kesef Mishneh).
he does not prefer this one over that one. He does not prefer one of the kinds over the others.
one of the seven species. Which have special importance, for which the Land of Israel is praised.
and whichever comes first in the verse takes precedence for the blessing. Because the Torah regarded it as important and placed it first.
dates take precedence over grapes etc.. The fruits describe the praise of the Land, so proximity to the word "land" is what determines precedence.
is the one for the grain species. The same as the "me'ein shalosh" (three-part summary) blessing recited over grain products (for its full text see above 3:13).
and over the fruits. And the vine too is included among the fruits.
its fruits. For these are fruits of the Land of Israel.
drank wine, ate dates, and ate a dish of the five species of grain. For all these foods one recites the "me'ein shalosh" blessing at the end.
over this by itself and over that by itself. "Me'ein shalosh" over the wine and "who creates many living beings" over the meat, since there is no way to include one of them in the other's blessing.

because they are all fruits of the tree. Therefore tree fruits that are not among the seven species are included in the "me'ein shalosh" blessing, although by themselves one recites "who creates many living beings" over them.
just as a person is forbidden to derive benefit from food or drink before reciting a blessing. For he is like one who derives benefit from a forbidden thing from consecrated property (above 1:2).
a tree or from a tree. That it is a tree or things that come from it (for the definition of a tree see Hilchot Kilayim 5:20).
myrrh, which comes from an animal. A perfumery substance extracted from the musk deer (see also Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 1:3).
"who creates various kinds of spices". A general blessing over fragrance that does not refer to its source of growth (compare the "by whose word all things came to be" blessing, above 8:1).
and over everything, if he said "who creates various kinds of spices" he has fulfilled his obligation. For it is a blessing that includes all kinds of spices (compare above 8:10).
incense. Spices that are burned on coals.
until its smoke rises. Until smoke comes out of it and the fragrance begins to rise, for before that there is not much enjoyment in its smell.
balsam oil. Oil that drips from the branches of the balsam shrub ("balm of Gilead", not the fruit known by this name today), or is produced from them by boiling.
"who creates fragrant oil". The blessing intended for oil that naturally gives off a pleasant smell.
until its scent became fragrant again. The oil's scent became stronger because of the process it underwent.
"who creates fragrant trees". Because this is a pleasant fragrance extracted from a tree. He does not recite "fragrant oil" since this is not a good, perfumed smell.
oil that he perfumed like the anointing oil. That he gave the oil a pleasant smell by cooking it with a mixture of various spices (see Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 1:2).
"who creates various kinds of spices". Because it contains spices of different kinds.
they brought oil before him. Olive oil, whose blessing is "fragrant trees".
he recites the blessing over the myrtle and exempts the oil. Because the main use of myrtle is smelling it, unlike oil, which is mainly meant for eating and anointing.
the blessing of one of them does not exempt the other. Because neither of them includes the other (compare above 8:10).
holds the wine in his right hand. Because of the importance of the blessing over the cup (see Hilchot Shabbat 29:7; and see also above 7:14).
and he smears it on the attendant's head. He needs to wipe the oil off his hands, so he smears it on the attendant's head to perfume his hair.
and if the attendant was a Torah scholar. Because of suspicion, it is not fitting for him to go out with perfumed hair (Hilchot De'ot 5:9).
he wipes it on the wall. Wipes the oil off on the wall.
something that is in doubt... "who creates various kinds of spices". This is a general blessing (see above halakhah 1).
the peddler. A seller of spices.
of many kinds. Different kinds of spices, whose blessings differ.
if he sat there the entire day... entered and left etc.. If he sat there all day, there is only one act of enjoyment; if he left and entered, he enjoys the smell anew each time.
and chilfei mayim. There are several identifications of this plant, and it seems to mean rosemary.
narcissus. Narcissus.
and of the field. That grows wild and is not like the cultivated kind.
and rose water. Perfumed water made from rose petals.
and frankincense. A fragrant resin that drips from the frankincense tree.
and mastic. A fragrant substance used as chewing gum, extracted from the resin of the mastic tree (see Hilchot Shabbat 21:24).
a fragrance that it is forbidden to smell etc.. Examples of these rules will be given in the next halakhah.
spices of idolatry. Which is forbidden for benefit, it and all its accessories and offerings (see Hilchot Avodah Zarah 7:2).

that are on a woman with whom relations are forbidden. Women who are forbidden to a man for relations. It is forbidden to smell spices on her, as a safeguard against forbidden relations (Hilchot Issurei Biah 21:2).
and oil made to remove filth. That is used for cleaning.
incense with which vessels are fumigated. Spices are burned on coals to give vessels and clothes a pleasant smell.
because it was not made to be smelled for its own sake as incense. Rather it was made to perfume the clothes.
for there is no main spice there. The substance from which the fragrance came is not present in them.
for a gentile banquet is presumed to be for idolatry. Therefore they have the law of idolatrous spices, which it is forbidden to smell (above halakhah 8).
outside the city. Outside the town.
if most of the city is gentiles he does not recite a blessing. The majority decides, and perhaps it is from idolatry.
and things that have no opening and no closing. Statements without the formula "Blessed are You, Lord..." at their beginning and end.
by way of praise and thanksgiving to the Holy One, blessed be He. And not a blessing over enjoyment or over a commandment (see above 1:3-4).
like the blessings of the prayer, which we have already written. Which are recited every day, and were written in Hilchot Tefillah 7:1-13.
whether he has others like them or does not. Even if he already has such vessels, he recites a blessing over the joy of the new vessels.
he recites "who has kept us alive". Over the joy of the meeting.
twelve months... "who revives the dead". So long a period has passed that one can forget in it, like a dead person who is forgotten from the heart.
a fruit that renews from year to year. That grows in an annual cycle and does not grow all year.
after thirty days. Which is a long period.
"who is good and does good". That He is good and does good to people.
"the true Judge". An acknowledgment that God judges with true judgment, even when the result is bad.
with a good heart. With composure.
even though the matters indicate that this good will cause him harm. For it is possible that harm will grow out of that good.
for we do not recite a blessing over what will be in the future. Lest the thing that is expected to happen does not come.
if he has a field he recites "who has kept us alive". Over the joy he has in the falling of the rain.
his own and others' he recites "who is good and does good". That He does good to him and to others (and see below halakhah 7).
"we give thanks to You" etc.. A general blessing of thanks for the benefit the world has from the falling of rain.
"Lord of most thanksgivings, God of praises". That abundant thanks are fitting for Him and He is praised with praises.
bubbles. Bubbles.
on the surface of the water. On top of the puddles.
and the bubbles go toward one another. Until they merge because of the abundance of water.
his father. Your father.
his father died and he inherited from him. For there is in the matter both bad news and good news.
if he has brothers with him he recites... "who is good and does good". The wording "does good" includes benefit to him and to others.
and if he has no brothers with him he recites "who has kept us alive". That is the individual's thanks for having reached that good (see also above halakhah 5).
the measure of the matter. The rule in this matter.
four must give thanks. To recite a special blessing for having been rescued from trouble.
and a prisoner. A captive.
and seafarers when they come up. When they reach dry land.
in the congregation of the people. That is, ten Israelites, as with any matter of sanctity (see Hilchot Tefillah 8:4-6).
and in the seat of the elders. That is, the Sages (see Hilchot Talmud Torah 6:1), the minimum of the plural being two.
"who bestows good things on the guilty, who has bestowed all good on me". He bestows good even on the wicked ("the guilty"), and has done me this good.
may He bestow good on you forever. May He continue to do good for you always.
the Red Sea. Which was split in two before the Israelites after the Exodus from Egypt (see Exodus 14:21-31).
and the crossings of the Jordan. Where the waters stood when the Israelites entered the land of Canaan (Joshua 3:15-17).
a place where a miracle was done for the many. Everyone who passes there must recite a blessing over it.
the lions' den. Into which Daniel was thrown and was saved from them (Daniel chapter 6).
and the fiery furnace. Into which Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah were thrown, and a miracle was done for them and they were saved from death (see Daniel chapter 3).
who gave patience to those who transgress His will. That He does not take revenge on them even though they transgress His will and worship idolatry.
and turn the hearts of their worshipers to serve You. That all will recognize God's kingship.
who sets the boundary of the widow. The Land of Israel has been like a widow since the destruction of the First Temple (see Lamentations 1:1), and it is being rebuilt.
who formed you in judgment etc.. All of God's acts are by true judgment (see above halakhah 3).
one who sees six hundred thousand people. That is, a multitude of people.
and in the Land of Israel. The significance of the Israelite population is specifically in the Land of Israel.
who knows secrets. Who knows what is in the secret recesses of the heart of each and every one of them.
who gave of His wisdom to flesh and blood. The wisdom he has is from the wisdom of the Holy One, blessed be He.
to those who fear Him. That is, Israel.
who gave of His glory to flesh and blood. The honor he has is from the honor of the Holy One, blessed be He.
who varies the creatures. That He also created creatures that are unusual compared with the norm.
and spotted ones. Whose skin has white blotches.
the true Judge. Over the deformities that occurred in them.
an elephant, a monkey, and an ape. These are special animals that resemble man to some degree.
beautiful and exceptionally well-formed. Beautiful in an extraordinary way.
for such is His way in His world. That there are such beautiful creatures in the world.
so that people may delight in them. To give people pleasure.
and over the noise of a rumbling heard in the earth like great millstones. The sound heard in an earthquake.
whose power fills the world. That God's power is evident in these things.
who makes the work of creation. For they are part of creation.
if he saw one of them after thirty days. That he does not see them regularly, but only occasionally.

who remembers the covenant, is faithful to His covenant, and keeps His word. The rainbow is the sign of the covenant between God and the earth, that the earth will not be destroyed as it was at the time of the Flood (see Genesis 9:13-17).
one who sees the moon in its renewal. Sees the moon anew after it disappeared at the end of the previous month.
their task. Their orbit.
their Maker. The Creator.
that it will be renewed as a crown of glory for those borne from the womb. The renewal of the moon is a good sign and a hint of glory for Israel, who are called "borne from the womb" (Isaiah 46:3).
for they are destined to be renewed like it. That although they sometimes decline, they will reach a high level and renewal.
standing. While standing.
as if he received the Shekhinah. The renewal of the moon hints at the renewal and redemption of Israel, who will in the future merit to receive the Shekhinah.
on the first night. On the first night of the month, immediately after the molad (birth) of the new moon.
until its blemish is filled. Until the whole moon shines.
the equinox of Nisan. The spring equinox.

the beginning of the twenty-eight-year cycle etc.. This time falls at the beginning of Tuesday night (the eve of Wednesday) once every twenty-eight years, when things return to the state they were in when the sun was created on the fourth day of creation (Hilchot Kiddush HaChodesh 9:4).
when the moon returns to the beginning of Aries at the beginning of the month etc.. That the molad of the month of Nisan falls at the time of the spring equinox.
and likewise when each of the other five planets returns. Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus and Mercury, which return to the beginning of their orbits at this time.
and likewise whenever Aries is seen rising from the end of the east. That this constellation is seen rising in the middle of the eastern side.
over each of these he recites "who makes the work of creation". Because it returns to the starting point.
the house of the proud the Lord will tear down. This is a prayer for their uprooting and destruction.
God of vengeance, Lord, God of vengeance. It is evident that God takes vengeance on His enemies (see above halakhah 9).
your mother is ashamed etc.. That there is no hope for the nations (above halakhah 11).
that You bring me in peace and take me out in peace. In the bathhouses there was expected danger if the partition between the fire and the place of the bathers were to collapse.
and the like of it in the future. From the fire of Gehinnom.
the fire. The fire.
to let blood. A medical procedure of drawing blood from the body.
to measure his threshing floor. To measure the amount of grain on the threshing floor.
in the heap. A pile of grain.
this is a vain prayer. Since the act has already been done, there is nothing more to ask for.
and anyone who cries out over the past. Prays for things that have already happened.
that I not stumble in a matter of halakhah. That I not err and rule halakhah incorrectly.
and my colleagues will rejoice in me. That they will be pleased with me.
from those who sit on street corners. Idle people who sit at street corners and chat.
to a city. A large central city, where danger might come.
opens them with "blessed" and closes them with "blessed". The opening of the blessing is "Blessed are You, Lord..." and its conclusion is likewise in this form.
except for the last blessing of the Shema. Which opens with "emet veyatziv" or "emet ve'emunah" (Hilchot Keriat Shema 1:6-7).
and a blessing that is adjacent to another. There is no need to open with the Name and God's kingship, because it relies on what was said in the preceding blessing (above 1:5).
and the blessing over fruits and the like, and the blessing over performing commandments. These are short blessings.

and these blessings that we mentioned etc.. The blessings of thanks mentioned in the previous chapter (and likewise the morning blessings of thanks, Hilchot Tefillah chapter 7); these too are not among those that open and close with "blessed".
except a few of the blessings over commandments. Except for a few of these blessings, in which this rule does apply.
such as the blessing over the Torah scroll. Which opens and closes with "blessed" (Hilchot Tefillah 12:5).
one who sees the graves of Israel. This too opens and closes with "blessed" (above 10:10).
but they are like optional. Their obligation depends on something else, and therefore there is no necessity that a person be obligated in those commandments.
in a tent or on a ship. Which are not permanent dwellings and are exempt from mezuzah (Hilchot Mezuzah 6:9).

and every positive commandment between a person and the Holy One, blessed be He... he recites a blessing over it. The blessing mentions that this act is a commandment of God, and is done with that in mind.
rabbinic. An enactment of the Sages.
eruv and washing the hands. Which one is obligated in only in certain cases.
"who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to". This is the same wording as the blessing over Torah commandments.
and where did He command us?. But these are enactments of the Sages.

the matter and its sense is as follows etc.. The word "and commanded us" should be explained thus: that He commanded us to obey the command of the Sages and to fulfill all their enactments (see also above 6:2; and see also Hilchot Mamrim 1:1-2).
washing the hands at the end. After the meal, which is meant to clean the hands of residues of salt, which is dangerous to the eyes (above 6:2-3).
because of the danger of a leech. Which is not visible at night, and to avoid drinking it the water must be strained.
for its performance still continues. The fulfillment of the commandment extends over time and is not a one-time act.
he recites the blessing after the performance. For he is still fulfilling the commandment.

for example, one who wrapped himself in tzitzit etc.. Here are examples of commandments whose performance continues even after the blessing: wrapping in tzitzit, putting on tefillin, and sitting in a sukkah.

but if he slaughtered etc.. These are examples of commandments performed by a one-time act: slaughtering, covering the blood, separating terumah and tithes, and immersion (see also Hilchot Ishut 3:23).
except for the immersion of the convert. In order for the gentile to become an Israelite he must immerse in a mikveh (see Hilchot Issurei Biah 13:1-7, 14:5-6).
for he has not yet been sanctified and has not been commanded. He has no commandment upon him as a gentile.
because he was excluded from the outset. At the outset he was not fit to recite a blessing, and therefore he recites it afterwards.
a commandment whose performance is the completion of its obligation. By the very preparation of the object of the commandment, he fulfills the commandment.
a commandment after whose performance there is another command. A command regarding use of the object, in addition to the commandment of preparing it.
if he made a parapet. Its construction is the completion of the commandment, and there is no other command after it.
every commandment that comes from time to time. Fixed in the cycle of time and not a daily obligation. And he gives thanks for having reached the time in which this commandment is observed.

every commandment that is an acquisition of his. That is carried out with things that are a person's property, and when he acquires such a new object he recites a blessing over it like over any new object (above 10:1).
a commandment that is not frequent and not found at all times. That one is obligated in only rarely.
for it is similar to a commandment that comes from time to time. That it is not a common, daily obligation, and one should give thanks for the opportunity to fulfill even this commandment.
he recites over it at the time of performance "who has kept us alive". For that is the beginning of the time of the commandment (compare above 10:2).
he recites over them "who has kept us alive" at the time he fulfills his obligation through them. For that is the main time of the commandment (and see Hilchot Sukkah 6:12).
one who performs it for others. In matters through which he can enable others to fulfill their obligation.

but he does not recite "who has kept us alive" except over a commandment that he performed for himself. A person does not have great joy at having reached the performance of a commandment unless it is for himself.
he does not recite... over the commandments. A general blessing over the commandments; this is not done because each commandment has importance in itself and is worthy of its own blessing.
if he performed it for himself he recites "to perform". For he himself is commanded to perform it.
for others he recites "on the performance of". He cannot recite "to perform" because the commandment does not apply to him directly.
put on tefillin etc.. These are examples of commandments that a person does for himself, and he recites "to perform".
if he affixed a mezuzah for others etc.. These are examples of commandments that a person may do for the sake of others.
if it was a commandment that is not an obligation. Its obligation depends on something else, and there is no necessity that a person be obligated in those commandments.
he recites "on the performance of". Because there is no positive commandment obligating that person to perform the commandment, since it is possible that he would not be obligated in it.
if it was an obligation. That there is an unconditional obligation to perform it.
he recites "to perform". For he is commanded to perform, and the others are included in his blessing.
he recites "on the taking of" the lulav. Even though it is a commandment that a person does for himself.

for once he has lifted it he has fulfilled his obligation. He does not recite "to take the lulav", because the sense of the wording "to take" is that he has not yet taken it. Rather he recites "on the taking of", a formulation that includes an act already done.

washing the hands and slaughtering, since they are in the nature of optional matters etc.. If he does not want to eat bread he is not commanded to wash his hands, and if he does not want meat he is not commanded to slaughter (above halakhah 3), so he is not commanded to perform.

for from the moment he resolved in his heart to nullify, the commandment of removal is fulfilled. From the moment he decided that he wants to nullify the leaven, it is nullified and as if removed, and so he cannot recite "to remove".

as will be explained in its place. Hilchot Chametz UMatzah 2:2. There it is explained that the "cessation" stated in the Torah is nullifying the leaven and regarding it as dust and as something of no use.
anything that is a custom... one does not recite a blessing over it. For it is not a commandment.
for it is a custom of the prophets. An ancient custom attributed to the prophets, but not an enactment of a commandment.
such as taking the willow on the seventh day of the festival. In the Temple on Sukkot, every day they brought willow branches and stood them upright around the altar (Hilchot Lulav 7:20-22).
a custom of the Sages. That they instituted this, but not as an enactment of a commandment.

reciting Hallel on Rosh Chodesh and on the intermediate days of Pesach. It is recited in a skipping, abbreviated form, since on those days it is read not as a commandment but as a custom (Hilchot Chanukah 3:7-8).
and likewise anything about which you have doubt... they do it without a blessing. Because blessings are rabbinic (above 1:1-2), and in cases of doubt we are lenient (above 4:2; 8:12).
a person should be careful about a blessing that is not needed. For it is like taking the Name of Heaven in vain (above 1:15).
and increase the blessings that are needed. For they are an expression of faith, praise, and thanksgiving to the Creator (above 1:3-4).
